summary: A circus strongman hauled statues to London, a French clerk founded Egypt's own museum: two faces of the 19th-century scramble for Egypt's past.
look: Belzoni's trail crosses yours: he cleared the sand from Abu Simbel's door (17th), found Seti I's tomb in the Valley (21st) and opened Khafre's pyramid at Giza (12th). Mariette's monument is the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, heir to the museum he founded, and he is buried in its front garden. Much of what you will not see in Egypt is in London, Paris and Turin because of this era.
story:
Under Muhammad Ali, antiquities were a collector's market. The British consul Henry Salt and the French consul Bernardino Drovetti competed for statues and coffins, now in the British Museum, the Louvre and Turin. Giovanni Belzoni, a 2-metre Paduan, had been a strongman in London's circuses. He came to Egypt in 1815 to sell the Pasha a water-raising machine, failed, and went to work for Salt. In 1816 he moved the 7-tonne 'Younger Memnon' bust of Ramesses II from the Ramesseum to the Nile in 17 days with 130 men. In 1817 he cleared Abu Simbel's entrance and found Seti I's tomb; in 1818 he entered Khafre's pyramid.

Auguste Mariette arrived in 1850 to buy manuscripts for the Louvre, spotted a sphinx in the sand at Saqqara and uncovered the Serapeum, the catacomb of the Apis bulls. In 1858 he became Egypt's first conservator of monuments, and in 1863 he opened a museum at Bulaq to keep finds in the country. He cleared Edfu and Dendera, rescued Queen Ahhotep's jewels from the Khedive's hands and sketched the plot of Aida, though he also kept Egyptians out of senior posts. Maspero and Petrie followed. Partage, the splitting of finds with foreign excavators, explains much of what is abroad.
details: Khafre's pyramid (12th): if it is open, look for Belzoni's name painted in big letters in the burial chamber, dated March 1818.
KV17, Seti I's tomb, is still nicknamed Belzoni's tomb; he made casts of its reliefs for a London exhibition in 1820.
Egyptian Museum, Tahrir: Mariette lies in a sarcophagus in the front garden, beside the collection he started.
Abu Simbel (17th): when Belzoni began digging, only the tops of the colossi's heads showed above the sand.
Partage, splitting finds between Egypt and foreign diggers, is why so much is in London, Paris, Turin and Berlin.
fun_fact: Before Egypt, Belzoni performed in London as a strongman billed as the Patagonian Samson.
narration: In the early 1800s, Egypt's antiquities were a free-for-all. The British and French consuls, Henry Salt and Bernardino Drovetti, raced each other to ship statues home, which is why London, Paris and Turin have such collections. Salt's star digger was Giovanni Belzoni from Padua, a 2-metre circus strongman who had come to sell the Pasha a water wheel. In 1816 he dragged the 7-tonne bust of Ramesses the Second from the Ramesseum to the Nile with 130 men. He cleared the sand from Abu Simbel's door, found Seti the First's tomb, and opened Khafre's pyramid. Exploring the mummy pits of Thebes, he admitted sitting on mummies that crumpled under him. A generation later, Auguste Mariette came to buy manuscripts for the Louvre and instead found the Serapeum at Saqqara. He stayed, became Egypt's first director of antiquities in 1858, and opened a museum so finds would stay in the country. He even wrote the story of Verdi's Aida. Inside Khafre's pyramid, look for Belzoni's name, painted in big letters in the burial chamber.

summary: An awkward draughtsman, a racing earl and a last-chance season found Tutankhamun; the newspapers then invented the curse.
look: On the 21st you can visit Carter's house near the entrance to the Valley and the tomb itself, KV62; at the GEM on the 11th, everything he catalogued is together for the first time. Harry Burton's black-and-white photographs, widely reproduced, show each piece exactly as Carter found it.
story:
Howard Carter, born in 1874, was the son of an artist and had little formal education. At 17 he went to Egypt to copy tomb scenes at Beni Hasan, then trained under Flinders Petrie at Amarna and recorded Hatshepsut's temple. In 1899 he became Inspector of Monuments for Upper Egypt. After the Saqqara Affair of 1905, when he backed Egyptian guards against French tourists and refused to apologise, he resigned and sold watercolours to survive. In 1907 Gaston Maspero introduced him to George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon, a wealthy collector who wintered in Egypt.

Carnarvon won the Valley of the Kings concession in 1914, after Theodore Davis had declared it exhausted. The war interrupted, and by 1922 Carnarvon was ready to stop; Carter persuaded him to fund one more season. On 4 November 1922 a step appeared under the remains of workmen's huts. On 26 November Carter peered through a hole by candlelight; the remembered reply is 'Yes, wonderful things', though his journal says 'Yes, it is wonderful'. With Harry Burton's photographs, Alfred Lucas's chemistry and Arthur Mace's help, clearing the tomb took until 1932. Carnarvon sold exclusive coverage to The Times, infuriating rival papers.

Carnarvon died in Cairo on 5 April 1923 of blood poisoning. The press supplied a curse, with tales of failing lights and a dog dying at Highclere; Arthur Conan Doyle spoke of 'elementals'. No curse is inscribed in the tomb. Carter died of Hodgkin's disease in London in 1939; after his death, objects from the tomb were found in his collection.
details: Carter's house (21st): near the road into the Valley, with his desk and darkroom; a replica of the tomb stands nearby.
He made the first hole with a chisel his grandmother had given him for his 17th birthday.
Carter numbered every object and group in the tomb; his record cards are still used by researchers.
Carter's gravestone in London quotes the alabaster Wishing Cup, which you can see at the GEM.
Genuine ancient tomb curses are rare, mostly in Old Kingdom private tombs, and none was found in Tutankhamun's.
fun_fact: A 2002 medical study of the Westerners present at the tomb's openings found they lived as long as those who were not; Lady Evelyn, who entered in 1922, died in 1980.
narration: Howard Carter was an artist's son with little schooling, who came to Egypt at 17 to copy tomb paintings. He rose to be an inspector of monuments, then lost the job in 1905 for siding with Egyptian guards against a group of rowdy French tourists and refusing to apologise. For a while he sold watercolours to visitors. His break came through Lord Carnarvon, a racing-mad earl who wintered in Egypt for his health. From 1914 they searched the Valley of the Kings, which another digger had declared exhausted. By 1922 Carnarvon wanted to stop. Carter talked him into one last season. On 4 November, a step was found beneath some old workmen's huts; one version credits a boy bringing water. On 26 November Carter held a candle to a hole in the sealed door. Can you see anything, asked Carnarvon. Yes, wonderful things, Carter is remembered as saying. It took him 10 years to empty the tomb. Then the curse began, though no curse is written anywhere in it. Carnarvon died in Cairo in April 1923, from an infected mosquito bite. Newspapers, angry that he had sold exclusive rights to The Times, filled the gap with tales of lights failing across Cairo and his dog howling in England. Carter, the man who actually opened the coffins, died in his London flat in 1939, aged 64. Look at any of Burton's photographs: every object was recorded before it moved.

summary: Egypt's year, its calendar, its taxes and even its name came from one event: the river rising every summer and leaving black mud behind.
look: You are travelling at what was once the height of the flood: in October the old Nile stood at its highest, with the fields under water. Look for the contrast the Egyptians named their land after: the black-green strip of farmland and the red-gold desert, often a single step apart. The stone stairways called Nilometers, at Elephantine and Kom Ombo, measured the rise.
story:
The flood came from the monsoon over the Ethiopian highlands, which swells the Blue Nile and the Atbara between May and August. The rise reached Aswan in early June and kept going into September, often peaking again in October, before falling to its low point the next June. Typical heights were about 14 metres at Aswan and 12 at Luxor. Farmers trapped the water in earth-banked basins for about 45 days, let the silt settle, drained it and sowed. A low flood meant famine, a high one swept villages away. Egyptians called the flood the arrival of Hapi, and myth said it was the tears of Isis for Osiris.

The civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days, grouped into three seasons: Akhet, the inundation, Peret, emergence, and Shemu, harvest or low water. Each month had three 10-day weeks; in the Ramesside period the royal tomb builders seem to have had the last two days of each week off. Five extra days, the epagomenal days, completed the year. With no leap year, the calendar drifted a day every four years against the seasons and against the dawn rising of Sirius, Sopdet to the Egyptians and Sothis to the Greeks, the ideal start of the year. Ptolemy III's Canopus Decree of 238 BC tried to add a leap day; Augustus finally imposed one, creating the Alexandrian calendar that survives as the Coptic calendar.

Nilometers recorded each year's height, which set tax expectations. The annual flood ended in 1970 with the Aswan High Dam.
details: Elephantine Nilometer (Aswan): a stone stairway down to the river, with measuring marks on its walls.
Kom Ombo (20th): the Nilometer is a round stone well with a staircase spiralling down, beside the temple.
Hapi, the flood god: a man with a fat belly and heavy breasts, often tying the plants of north and south together.
Kom Ombo's calendar relief lists festival offerings month by month through the three seasons.
From a boat or car window, watch the sharp line where irrigated green stops and desert starts.
fun_fact: Julius Caesar's calendar reform was advised by a Greek astronomer from Alexandria, Sosigenes, so Egypt's 365-day year is an ancestor of the calendar on your phone.
narration: Imagine Egypt without rain. Every drop of water came down the Nile, and every summer it brought a gift. Monsoon rains fell on the mountains of Ethiopia, the river swelled, and from June the flood crept north past Aswan, peaking around September and October. In an ancient October like this one, the fields around you would be a sheet of brown water. When it drained, it left a layer of black silt so rich that the Egyptians named their country Kemet, the black land, as opposed to Deshret, the red land of the desert. Herodotus called Egypt the gift of the river. The flood shaped time itself. The year had 3 seasons of 4 months: Akhet, the flood, Peret, when the fields emerged and crops grew, and Shemu, the harvest and low water. Each month had 30 days, and 5 extra days at the end were the birthdays of the gods. That made 365 days but no leap year, so the calendar slowly drifted away from the seasons and from the dawn rising of Sirius, the star that in theory opened the year. The Coptic calendar, still used by farmers today, descends from it. Officials measured each flood on stone stairways called Nilometers and set taxes by the result. Since the High Dam was finished in 1970, the flood no longer comes. Look at the edge of the green: you can often stand with one foot in the black land and one in the red.

summary: Most of the year the gods stayed hidden; on festival days they came out in golden boats, and the whole city celebrated, prayed and visited its dead.
look: Festival scenes cover the walls you visit on the 21st and 22nd. A model boat with a cabin shrine, carried on poles by priests, is a god on an outing. The Opet procession runs along the walls of Luxor Temple's colonnade, the festival of Min fills a wall of Medinet Habu's second court, and Karnak's White Chapel was built for a king's jubilee.
story:
Festivals were when the gods became visible. Statues travelled in portable barques, model boats with a cabin shrine, carried on priests' shoulders or floated on gilded river barges. Ordinary people could approach, put yes-or-no questions to the god's oracle and share in the food.

The Sed festival, or 'Feast of the Tail', renewed a king after 30 years on the throne and every three or four years after that. He ran a ritual course between boundary markers and was enthroned twice, for Upper and Lower Egypt. Djoser's Sed court at Saqqara and Senusret I's White Chapel at Karnak were built for it. Hatshepsut and Akhenaten held theirs early; Ramesses II held 13 or 14.

Opet, in the second month of the flood season, took Amun, Mut and Khonsu from Karnak to Luxor Temple, where the king was reborn as Amun's son; it lasted 11 days under Thutmose III and 27 by the death of Ramesses III. The Beautiful Festival of the Valley, held at the new moon of the second month of Shemu, carried Amun across to the West Bank temples. Families brought flowers, food and drink to their relatives' tombs, feasting and sleeping beside the dead.
details: Luxor Temple colonnade (22nd): the Opet reliefs show the barques towed upriver, with musicians, dancers and butchers.
The heb-sed sign: a double pavilion with two thrones back to back, for the king's double enthronement.
Medinet Habu second court (21st): the festival of Min, with priests releasing birds to the four directions.
Karnak White Chapel (22nd): built for Senusret I's jubilee; its pillars show the king with the gods, above all Min.
Portable barque: a model boat with a cabin shrine, carried on poles by priests. Wherever you see it, a god is out.
fun_fact: Hathor's Festival of Drunkenness remembered how Ra saved humanity from the raging goddess with beer dyed red, which she drank until she fell asleep.
narration: Most of the year, Egypt's gods lived hidden in dark sanctuaries. On festival days they came out. Priests carried the god's statue in a gilded model boat on poles, and the whole town lined the route. The biggest festival in Thebes was Opet, in the flood season, when Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu travelled from Karnak to Luxor Temple, about 2 kilometres. Under Thutmose the Third it lasted 11 days; under Ramesses the Third, more than 3 weeks. Luxor still carries a boat in procession for its saint, Abu el-Haggag, an echo many see of Opet. The Beautiful Festival of the Valley took Amun across the river to the West Bank temples. Families followed with flowers, food and wine, and feasted at their relatives' tombs, sometimes staying the night. Then there was the Sed festival, the king's jubilee after 30 years, when he ran a ritual course to prove he was still fit to rule. Ramesses the Second held 13 or 14 of them. Look for the boat on poles: wherever it appears, a festival is under way.

summary: Bread with grit in it, beer you could almost chew, eyeliner for everyone: what ordinary Egyptian life tasted, smelled and looked like.
look: You will see daily life in the tombs of the nobles and at Deir el-Medina on the 21st, and in museum cases: model bakeries and breweries, wigs, mirrors, kohl tubes, sandals and board games. In the paintings, look for banquet guests wearing cones on their heads, and long lines of servants carrying loaves, ducks and jars.
story:
Bread and beer were the twin staples, and wages too. Bread was mostly of emmer wheat, pounded, sieved and ground on a saddle quern; by the New Kingdom loaves were slapped onto the inside of cylindrical clay ovens. Grit from the querns wore teeth down badly. Beer was thick, cloudy and nourishing, brewed from lightly baked bread or from malted grain, and still has a cousin in Egyptian bouza. Onions, garlic, leeks, lettuce, lentils, chickpeas, dates and figs filled out the diet; fish and birds were within most people's reach, beef mainly for the rich and for festivals. Geese were force-fed from about 2500 BC.

People wore linen, from simple kilts to fine pleated dresses. Men and women lined their eyes with kohl and wore wigs and jewellery, and banquet guests in paintings wear cones on their heads, perhaps of perfumed fat or wax. Medical papyri such as the Ebers and Edwin Smith papyri cover wounds, fractures and remedies, including honey dressings. People played senet and mehen, made music with harps, lutes, flutes and the rattling sistrum, and kept cats, dogs and monkeys as pets. A scribe ranked above all manual workers, and schoolbooks never let boys forget it.
details: TT52, Nakht (21st): a blind harpist and banquet guests with cones on their heads; TT69, Menna: harvest and field measuring.
TT100, Rekhmire: brick-making, metalwork and bread-making, a whole estate's workshops in one tomb.
Senet: a board of 30 squares in three rows of 10. Tutankhamun took several sets with him.
Kohl pots: little tubes or jars with an applicator stick, in stone, glass or faience, in every museum.
Middle Kingdom models: women grinding grain and men straining beer mash in tiny wooden bakeries and breweries.
fun_fact: Foie gras is Egyptian: tomb reliefs from about 2500 BC already show servants force-feeding geese.
narration: Here is how ordinary Egyptians lived. They ate bread at every meal, made from emmer wheat or barley, ground on stone querns. Grit from the stones got into the flour, and mummies show badly worn teeth. They drank beer every day, thick and cloudy, more like liquid bread, and workmen were paid partly in loaves and jugs of it. Add onions, garlic, lentils, dates and figs; fish and ducks for most people, beef for the rich. They wore linen, and both men and women lined their eyes with kohl. In banquet paintings, guests wear cones on their heads, which may have been scented fat or wax; nobody is quite sure. Doctors wrote textbooks on papyrus and dressed wounds with honey, and one pregnancy test had a woman pass urine on seeds of barley and wheat: if they sprouted, a baby was on the way. Children and adults played senet, a race game you will see among Tutankhamun's treasures. Look for the bread on any offering table: the loaves come in a dozen shapes.

period: c. 3100 BC to the Roman period
summary: Egyptian artists were not failing at perspective: they drew each body part from its clearest angle, by rules that held for 3,000 years.
look: Every relief on this trip follows the same rules, so learn them once and you can read any wall. A face in profile with a frontal eye, shoulders square to you, hips and legs in profile; the most important figure is the biggest. Scenes run in horizontal strips, each on its own ground line. Standing statues step forward on the left foot and stare straight ahead.
story:
Egyptian had no word for 'art'. Images did a job: to depict something was to make it last, so pictures had to be complete and unmistakable. Each part is shown from its most characteristic angle, which Egyptologists call aspective: a profile head with a frontal eye, frontal shoulders, and hips and legs in profile. Rank decides size, so kings dwarf servants and enemies. Scenes sit in horizontal registers on baselines; people further away are placed higher up or overlapped, not shrunk. Frontality, hierarchy of scale and composite views held from the 1st Dynasty to the Roman period.

Consistency came from method. Draughtsmen snapped a red grid onto the wall; a standing figure measured 18 squares from hairline to soles, and from the 25th and 26th Dynasties a revised 21-square grid was used. A sketch in red was corrected in black, then sculptors cut the relief and painters filled it with mineral colours. Work was done by teams, and most artists are anonymous, though Deir el-Medina's craftsmen left their names on their own tombs.

Colour followed convention: men reddish brown, women paler yellow, gods with golden skin and blue hair, Osiris green or black for growth and fertile silt. Raised relief suited interiors; sunk relief caught the strong sun outside. Statues were homes for the ka: frontal, backed by a pillar, eyes sometimes inlaid with rock crystal. The rules bent under Akhenaten, then returned, and later dynasties deliberately copied Old Kingdom models.
details: KV57, Horemheb (21st): unfinished walls show red grid lines, sketches corrected in black, and carving at every stage.
Hands: on many figures both hands are drawn as left or both as right, because clarity beat anatomy.
Statues: the man steps forward with his left foot; a woman usually stands with her feet together or barely apart.
Compare an outer wall with an inner hall at Karnak or Edfu: sunk relief outside, raised relief inside.
Rahotep and Nofret, in the museum: his reddish skin, her pale skin and their inlaid crystal eyes show the code in 3D.
fun_fact: One Egyptian word used for a sculptor meant 'he who makes alive', because a finished statue could house a living spirit.
narration: Egyptian artists could draw what they saw; they chose not to. A picture was meant to work forever, so every part had to be shown in its clearest view. A face is clearest in profile, but an eye is clearest from the front, so you get a frontal eye in a side face. Shoulders are clearest square on, hips and legs from the side. Egyptologists call this aspective rather than perspective. Size shows rank, not distance: the king towers, his wife may reach his knee, and enemies and servants are tiny. Scenes run in strips, like a comic, each on its own baseline. To keep proportions steady, draughtsmen drew a grid: a standing figure was 18 squares from the hairline to the soles, and from the 7th century BC, 21 squares. A draughtsman sketched in red, a master corrected in black, then sculptors and painters followed, mostly anonymous. Colour had rules too. Men are reddish brown, women pale yellow. Gods have flesh of gold and hair of lapis blue. Osiris can be green or black, the colours of new growth and fertile mud. Indoors they used raised relief; outside, sunk relief, which casts sharp shadows in the Egyptian sun. A statue was a body for the spirit, so it faces straight ahead, backed by a pillar. Only under Akhenaten did the rules bend. Look at the nearest figure: find the frontal eye, the square shoulders and the striding foot.

summary: Small notes, a smile and a firm 'la, shukran' will carry you through every temple, souq and felucca landing in Egypt.
look: You will meet baksheesh everywhere: the guard who unlocks a side chamber, the toilet attendant, the man who poses with his camel, the boy who 'shows' you the way. Touts gather at site entrances, in souqs and at boat landings. Carry small notes in a separate pocket and decide in advance what you are willing to pay.
story:
Baksheesh comes from the Persian bakhshesh, a gift, and across the Middle East it can mean a tip, alms or a bribe. Travellers have written about it for centuries: Mark Twain, riding through Galilee in 1867, described being mobbed by cries of 'bucksheesh'. In today's Egypt it mostly means a small tip for a small service, and it matters because many wages are low.

Expect to tip toilet attendants, hotel porters, drivers, felucca and boat crews, and site guards who unlock or light something for you. A guard offering to let you into a closed area, or to let you photograph where it is forbidden, is asking you to break the rules, and you can say no. Keep small notes in a separate pocket, and ask your guide or hotel what is normal this year, since prices have been changing fast.

Touts work with polite stories. The temple is closed, but there is a shop; the scarab is a gift, until it is not; the friendly stranger is 'not a guide'. A smile, 'la shukran' and walking on usually ends it; 'khalas', enough, closes the matter. Tour stops at papyrus, perfume and alabaster 'institutes' earn commissions: enjoy the tea, buy only what you want. For camels, horses, carriages and feluccas, agree the total, the number of people, the time and the return trip first, and pay at the end.

Respect the sites: no flash on paintings, no touching reliefs, photo permits where required. In mosques remove shoes, cover shoulders and knees, women cover their hair, and avoid Friday midday prayers.
details: Phrases: la shukran, no thank you; shukran, thank you; khalas, enough; salam aleikum, hello; ma'a salama, goodbye.
Camel, horse or felucca: agree the total price, number of people, duration and return trip before you start; pay at the end.
Photo rules vary by site and change often: check what your ticket covers, and never use flash on paintings.
Shopping stops for papyrus, perfume and alabaster pay guides a commission: drink the tea, buy only what you love.
Mosques: avoid Friday midday prayers; shoes off at the door; scarves or robes are often available at the entrance.
fun_fact: Baksheesh has puzzled visitors for centuries: Mark Twain, riding through Galilee in 1867, said the chorus of 'bucksheesh!' was the worst storm he had ever been in.
narration: Baksheesh is a Persian word that covers a tip, a gift to the poor and a little grease for the wheels, and in Egypt you will meet all three. Wages are low and small tips keep many people going, so treat it as part of the cost of travel, not as an insult. Keep a separate pocket of small notes, 5, 10 and 20 pounds, so you never flash a full wallet. Expect to tip toilet attendants, porters, drivers and boat crews. A guard who unlocks a side room or points his torch at a hidden relief will also expect something. Ask your guide what the going rate is this year, because prices move fast. Touts are the other half of the game. Someone tells you the temple is closed today, but his cousin's shop is open. Someone hands you a scarab as a free gift, then wants paying. Smile, say la shukran, no thank you, and keep walking. Khalas means enough, finished. For camels, horses, carriages and feluccas, agree the total price, per person or for everyone, how long, and whether the ride back is included, all before you climb on. Pay at the end. In mosques, take off your shoes, cover shoulders and knees, and women cover their hair. Do not touch painted walls: skin oil and salt damage the colours. Egyptians are warm and love a joke, so be firm, be kind, and laugh. Right now, check that you have small notes in an easy pocket.

summary: From Cretan envoys to Cavafy's Alexandria, Greeks have been in Egypt for about 3,500 years, and the words pyramid and obelisk are Greek.
look: The Greek layer is everywhere on this trip: Siwa's oracle of Ammon on the 13th-15th, Greek graffiti at Abu Simbel on the 17th, Philae and the Ptolemaic temples of the 20th, the Colossi of Memnon on the 21st. Look for Greek letters scratched or carved into stone. Read them aloud: you are reading what Greeks wrote there 2,000 to 2,600 years ago.
story:
Contacts are older than Classical Greece. Minoan-style frescoes decorated a palace at Avaris in the Delta, and around 1450 BC the vizier Rekhmire's tomb at Thebes shows Keftiu, usually identified as Cretans, bringing gifts. In the 7th century BC Psamtik I hired Ionian and Carian mercenaries, and Greek traders were based at Naukratis, on the Canopic branch of the Nile. Mercenaries campaigning in Nubia around 591 BC cut Greek graffiti into the colossi at Abu Simbel.

Herodotus of Halicarnassus travelled in Egypt in the mid 5th century BC. Book II of his Histories, the first long description of Egypt by an outsider, mixes sharp observation, priests' tales and errors, and is still quoted, not least for 'the gift of the river'. Alexander arrived in 332 BC, and for three centuries Egypt was ruled from Greek Alexandria; later Plutarch wrote the fullest ancient account of Isis and Osiris. Greek gave the world the names pyramid, obelisk, sphinx and hieroglyph.

In modern times a large Greek community, the Egyptiotes, flourished in Alexandria and Cairo, with schools, newspapers, clubs and pastry shops. The poet Constantine Cavafy was born in Alexandria in 1863. The community shrank sharply after the 1950s, but churches, the Patriarchate of Alexandria and a smaller community remain.
details: Abu Simbel (17th): Greek, Carian and Phoenician graffiti on the legs of the colossi by the door, cut around 591 BC.
Colossi of Memnon (21st): Greek verses by Roman-era visitors, among them the poet Julia Balbilla, on the northern statue.
Rekhmire's tomb, TT100: the Keftiu wear long hair and patterned kilts and carry Aegean-style vessels.
Greek words around you: pyramid, obelisk, sphinx, hieroglyph, papyrus; even Egypt comes from the Greek Aigyptos.
Siwa (13th-15th): the oracle the Greeks knew as Zeus-Ammon, consulted by Alexander in 331 BC.
fun_fact: Herodotus says an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded 1,600 silver talents spent on radishes, onions and garlic for the workers; his interpreter was probably improvising.
narration: As a Greek, you are not a stranger here. Around 1450 BC, men called Keftiu, probably Cretans, were painted bringing gifts in a vizier's tomb at Thebes. In the 600s BC, Egyptian kings hired Greek soldiers, and Greek merchants got their own town in the Delta, Naukratis. Around 591 BC, Greek mercenaries on campaign up the Nile carved their names on the colossi at Abu Simbel, where you can still read them. Herodotus came in the 5th century BC and wrote the first real guidebook to Egypt, half brilliant, half gossip. Then came Alexander, the Ptolemies and Alexandria. Your language named the sights: pyramid probably comes from a Greek word for a wheat cake, obelisk from a little roasting spit, and hieroglyph means sacred carving. In modern times a large Greek community lived in Alexandria and Cairo, and the poet Cavafy was born in Alexandria in 1863. A smaller community remains. Try saying ana min el-Yunan, I am from Greece, and watch the smiles. Look for Greek letters on old stones: you can read them.
